data.about: A cable bridge with its geometry given: two hangers carry the deck loads up to a cable slung between two anchors. Because the shape is given, the force diagram is fully determined — the rays parallel to the three cable segments meet in one pole, and the steepest segment carries the largest force. That force is then dimensioned: the required diameter in S235, and the axial force proof for a Ø18 mm S355 cable.

steps.caption: EX 2 task 2: a cable bridge whose shape is GIVEN — find the biggest cable force, then dimension the cable for it
steps.title: The exercise

steps.caption: left: two anchors, a cable in three segments, two hangers down to the deck — every length is given, so nothing about the shape is ours to choose
steps.title: The bridge

steps.caption: left: F₁d and F₂d hang from the deck and travel up the hangers into the cable nodes — right: the same two forces laid off tip to tail, the load line
steps.title: The loads

steps.caption: right: draw a ray parallel to the FIRST cable segment through the top of the load line, and one parallel to the LAST segment through its bottom — they cross at the pole o. Its distance from the load line is the horizontal thrust H
steps.title: The shape fixes the pole

steps.caption: right: the third ray, from o to the division between the loads — left: it comes out parallel to the middle cable segment, which proves the drawn shape really is the funicular of these two loads
steps.title: The middle ray checks it

steps.caption: left: each segment flashes — right: its force is the ray from the pole, all three in tension
steps.title: The three cable forces

steps.caption: the STEEPEST segment carries the most: it has the same horizontal thrust as the others but the largest vertical part. That segment governs the whole cable
steps.title: a) The relevant force

steps.caption: with the relevant force known, the formulary does the rest: A_req = N_d / f_td and f_td = f_tk / γ_M
steps.title: b) The required diameter

steps.caption: the axial force proof asks one question: is the force the cable must carry smaller than the force it can carry?
steps.title: c) The proof for Ø18 in S355
